title: The tree that bleeds and lives
hook: strike a great tree anywhere and it lives; why Hindus say the self does not die
carry: the body dies; the self does not

segments.voice: Yesterday: samudra, rivers that run from sea to sea. Your line was we come from Being, and go back.
screen: `SAMUDRA — WE COME FROM BEING, AND GO BACK.`

segments.voice: Find an old tree with a scar: where a branch was cut, or a car hit it, or someone carved initials years ago. Often you'll see where the sap ran, dried now into a hard, shiny crust. The tree bled. And it's still standing, still leafing out every spring. Next to it, maybe, one branch is gray and bare, and never came back. Same tree. One part alive, one part not. Uddalaka points his son to a great tree.
screen: `AN OLD TREE WITH A SCAR.` → `IT BLED, AND IT'S STILL STANDING.` → `ONE GRAY BRANCH.`

segments.voice: If someone were to strike this great tree at its root, my dear, Uddalaka says, it would bleed sap, but it would live. Strike it in the middle, it would bleed, but live. Strike it at the top, it would bleed, but live. Filled through and through by the living self, the jiva atman, it stands, drinking in water, rejoicing. But if life leaves one branch, that branch dries up. If it leaves a second, or a third, they dry up. If it leaves the whole tree, the whole tree dries up. Then the line that turns it toward his son. In the same way, my dear, understand this: the body dies when life leaves it. But life does not die. Look at the order. The body depends on the self, not the other way around. A dry branch isn't the death of life; it's life leaving that branch. This is one of Hinduism's central teachings: the atman, the self, is not the body, and it does not die. The Bhagavad Gita says it too, in its second chapter: as a person puts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body. That is the hope many Hindu families hold onto at a funeral. They grieve, truly. And they say: the body has died; the one we love has not. Then the refrain once more: you are that, Shvetaketu.
screen: `STRIKE IT: IT BLEEDS, BUT LIVES.` · `LIFE LEAVES A BRANCH; IT DRIES.` · `THE ATMAN IS NOT THE BODY.` · `WORN-OUT CLOTHES, PUT OFF.` · then, large: `THE BODY DIES. THE SELF DOES NOT.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to your feet, your roots, and feel something alive there: warmth, tingling, a pulse. Move up through your belly and chest, where the breath moves, to your face and scalp, the same life from root to crown, and rest in it the way the tree stands, drinking in water.
The tree. Uddalaka's great tree, filled by the living self: wounded, it lives; when life leaves, it dries; the body dies, but the self does not.
Your line: the body dies; the self does not. That's day three hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: At Hindu deathbeds and funerals, families may recite or reflect on scriptures that teach that the self does not die with the body, from the Upanishads to the Bhagavad Gita's second chapter.

chat.says: Sam's grandpa died last night 💔 he texted 'is he just gone?' what do i even say
options: i'm so sorry. in my family we believe the self doesn't die with the body. like Uddalaka's tree: life leaves, but it doesn't die.

chat.meaning: Uddalaka's tree bleeds but lives; when life leaves, the body dies, but life does not. Hindus hold that the self, the atman, does not die.

tie.story: Uddalaka told his son that when life leaves a tree it dries up, but life itself does not die.
tie.friend: Priya can be sorry with Sam first, then share her tradition's hope: his grandpa's body died, his self did not.
tie.you: what do you hope about someone you've lost?

atman.meaning: the self, which does not die with the body
